{{Short description|Concept in atmospheric dynamics and physical oceanography}}
{{Refimprove|date=December 2009}}

In [[atmospheric dynamics]] and physical [[oceanography]], the '''Rossby radius of deformation''' is the length scale at which rotational effects become as important as [[buoyancy]] or [[gravity wave]] effects in the evolution of the [[Fluid dynamics|flow]] about some disturbance.<ref>Gill, A. E., 1982: Atmosphere-Ocean Dynamics, Academic Press, Orlando, 662 pp.</ref>

For a [[barotropic]] [[ocean]], the Rossby radius is <math>L_R \equiv \frac{(gD)^{1/2}}{f}</math>, where <math>g</math> is the [[gravitational acceleration]], <math>D</math> is the water depth, and <math>\,f</math> is the [[Coriolis parameter]].<ref>Cushman-Roisin, B. & Beckers, J.M., 2011: Introduction to Geophysical Fluid Dynamics, Academic Press, Waltman, p. 275</ref>

For ''f'' = {{val|1|e=-4|u=s-1}} appropriate to 45° latitude, ''g'' = 9.81&nbsp;m/s<sup>2</sup> and ''D'' = 4&nbsp;km, ''L''<sub>R</sub> &asymp; 2000&nbsp;km; using the same latitude and gravity but changing ''D'' to 40&nbsp;m; ''L''<sub>R</sub> &asymp; 200&nbsp;km.

The ''n''th [[baroclinic]] Rossby radius is:
: <math>L_{R, n} \equiv \frac{NH}{n \pi f_0}</math>, where <math>N</math> is the [[Brunt–Väisälä frequency]], <math>H</math> is the [[scale height]], and ''n'' = 1, 2, ...&nbsp;.

In Earth's atmosphere, the ratio ''N''/''f''<sub>0</sub> is typically of order 100, so the Rossby radius is about 100 times the vertical scale height, ''H''. For a vertical scale associated with the height of the [[tropopause]], ''L''<sub>R,1</sub> &asymp; 1000&nbsp;km, which is the predominant scale seen on weather charts for [[cyclones]] and [[anticyclones]]. This is commonly called the [[synoptic scale meteorology|synoptic scale]].   

In the ocean, the baroclinic Rossby radius varies dramatically with latitude. Near the equator it is larger than 200&nbsp;km, while in the high latitude regions it is less than 10&nbsp;km.<ref>Chelton, D. B., DeSzoeke, R. A., Schlax, M. G., El Naggar, K., & Siwertz, N. (1998). Geographical Variability of the First Baroclinic Rossby Radius of Deformation. Journal of Physical Oceanography, 28(3), 433–460. doi:10.1175/1520-0485(1998)028<0433:GVOTFB>2.0.CO;2</ref><ref> Nurser, A. J. G., & Bacon, S., 2014, The Rossby radius in the Arctic Ocean, Ocean Sci., 10, 967–975, doi: 10.5194/os-10-967-2014</ref> The size of ocean eddies varies similarly; in low latitude regions, near the equator, eddies are much larger than in high latitude regions.

The associated dimensionless parameter is the [[Rossby number]]. Both are named in honor of [[Carl-Gustav Rossby]].
